title: Feedback-driven iteration
use_cases: Implement when narrative outputs require progressive refinement through repeated critique-revision cycles
Configure when specific narrative dimensions like emotional depth or coherence need targeted improvement
Use when building multi-agent systems that mimic human collaborative writing workflows
Apply when managing concise creative formats that benefit from bounded iterative feedback loops
Use when defining automated stop conditions based on evaluation score convergence or quality thresholds
content: Feedback-driven iteration forms the foundational mechanism of self-adaptation in multi-agent AI systems applied to creative writing, enabling progressive refinement of narrative outputs through repeated cycles of generation, evaluation, critique, and revision.[1] The typical structure begins with an initial draft or idea generated by one or more agents, followed by evaluation against specific quality criteria, critique that identifies targeted weaknesses or opportunities for improvement, and subsequent revision that incorporates the resulting insights into a new iteration. This loop repeats, allowing the system to incrementally enhance aspects of the narrative while building on prior outputs.[1] Targeted feedback distinguishes these systems by concentrating each cycle on particular narrative dimensions—such as emotional depth, coherence, linguistic quality, or adherence to the prompt—rather than attempting broad improvements simultaneously.[1] By focusing revisions on one or a few metrics at a time, the process enables precise adjustments that accumulate into substantial gains in overall story quality, creativity, and contextual richness, mimicking the incremental refinement found in human collaborative writing processes.[1] Iteration continues until termination conditions are satisfied, which may include completing a predetermined number of cycles, reaching convergence in evaluation scores, or achieving a predefined quality threshold; in some cases, human oversight provides the final stop condition.[1] These systems are particularly effective when applied to concise formats such as flash fiction, where the bounded scope allows iterative feedback to efficiently balance creativity with coherence and narrative focus.[1]
